title: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?

s1_definition.profdef: A primary key uniquely identifies every row in a table and cannot be null; a table has exactly one primary key, which the database backs with a unique index and treats as the default target for foreign keys. A unique key (unique constraint) also enforces that values are not duplicated, but a table can have many unique keys and, in most databases, a unique column may hold one null value because null is treated as unknown rather than equal to another null.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's account number SAV2001 is his primary key — it is the official, never-null, one-and-only way the bank identifies his account, and every ledger entry points back to it. His registered email and his PAN are unique keys — no two customers can share the same email or PAN, so they are unique, but they are not the identity the whole system is built around, and a customer might not have given an email yet, so that column can be empty while the account still exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: One primary key per table, never null, the row's identity and foreign-key target; many unique keys allowed, one null typically permitted, enforcing no-duplicates on other columns.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A primary key uniquely identifies every row in a table and cannot be null; a table has exactly one primary key, which the database backs with a unique index and treats as the default target for foreign keys. A unique key (unique constraint) also enforces that values are not duplicated, but a table can have many unique keys and, in most databases, a unique column may hold one null value because null is treated as unknown rather than equal to another null.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's account number SAV2001 is his primary key — it is the official, never-null, one-and-only way the bank identifies his account, and every ledger entry points back to it. His registered email and his PAN are unique keys — no two customers can share the same email or PAN, so they are unique, but they are not the identity the whole system is built around, and a customer might not have given an email yet, so that column can be empty while the account still exists.

**One line to remember:** One primary key per table, never null, the row's identity and foreign-key target; many unique keys allowed, one null typically permitted, enforcing no-duplicates on other columns.

sections.s2_technical:
Both a primary key and a unique key guarantee uniqueness and both are enforced by a unique index, so for lookups they behave similarly. The differences are about identity, nullability, and count. A primary key is the chosen identity of the row. There can be only one per table because a row can have only one canonical identity. It is implicitly `NOT NULL`, because an identity that is unknown is meaningless. And by convention and tooling, foreign keys from other tables point at the primary key, and in many databases the primary key also determines physical clustering order on disk.

A unique key enforces that no two rows share the same value in the constrained column or set of columns, but it is not the row's identity. A table can have any number of unique keys. For example an accounts table might have the account id as primary key and separate unique constraints on email and on PAN. Nullability is the subtle part: the SQL standard treats null as "unknown," and two unknowns are not considered equal, so most databases allow multiple rows with null in a unique column, though they allow at most one null per unique single-column constraint depending on the database. PostgreSQL permits multiple nulls in a unique column; some other engines differ, so this is a point to state carefully in an interview.

In practice you declare a primary key with `PRIMARY KEY` and a unique key with `UNIQUE`. A senior nuance is the design choice of what to make the primary key. Even when a natural unique attribute like email exists, teams usually make the primary key a surrogate — an auto-increment or UUID with no business meaning — and keep email as a unique constraint, because the primary key should be stable and meaningless while business attributes change. Another nuance is that composite uniqueness is common: a unique constraint can span multiple columns, for example unique on the pair of customer id and account type so a customer cannot open two savings accounts, and a primary key can likewise be composite. Both the primary key and unique keys speed up lookups because of their backing indexes, but only the primary key carries the special identity and default foreign-key semantics.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must identify each account with one stable, never-null handle that every transaction and statement references. If that handle could be null or could change, the whole ledger would break. This is exactly the role of a primary key.

Problem 2 — The bank must also guarantee that no two customers register the same email and that no two accounts use the same PAN, yet a brand-new account might not have an email on file yet. This is exactly a unique key: it forbids duplicates but tolerates an unknown value.

The mini-project creates an accounts table with the account id as the primary key and unique constraints on email and PAN, then a small Java validator that inserts accounts and demonstrates that a duplicate account id is rejected as a primary-key violation, a duplicate email is rejected as a unique violation, and a null email is accepted.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,         -- primary key: identity, NOT NULL, only one
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email       VARCHAR(120) UNIQUE,             -- unique key: no dup, but NULL allowed
    pan         CHAR(10)     UNIQUE,             -- another unique key
    acct_type   VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    -- composite unique: a customer cannot open two accounts of the same type
    CONSTRAINT uq_holder_type UNIQUE (holder_name, acct_type)
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, holder_name, email, pan, acct_type, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 'rajesh@example.com', 'ABCDE1234F', 'SAVINGS', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 'priya@example.com',  'PQRSX6789K', 'CURRENT',  250000.00);
```

```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/key-constraints-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Inspect the keys on the table
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three insert attempts against an accounts table that already holds SAV2001 (Rajesh) and CUR3001 (Priya).

Step 1: The first insert reuses the id SAV2001. The database checks the primary-key index, finds SAV2001 already present, and rejects the insert as a primary-key violation. No row is added.

Step 2: The second insert uses a fresh id SAV2002 but reuses Rajesh's email. The id passes the primary-key check, but the unique index on email finds a duplicate and rejects the insert. No row is added.

Step 3: The third insert uses a fresh id SAV2003 and a null email. The id is unique, and the unique email constraint allows the null because null is treated as unknown, not as a duplicate. The row is added successfully.

Step 4: The table now has three accounts, proving that the primary key enforces unique never-null identity while the unique key enforces no-duplicate values yet tolerates null.

```text
Feb 14,2026 10:20:00 SEVERE AccountDao - Rejected SAV2001: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "accounts_pkey"
Feb 14,2026 10:20:00 SEVERE AccountDao - Rejected SAV2002: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "accounts_email_key"
Feb 14,2026 10:20:00 INFO  AccountDao - Inserted account SAV2003
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A primary key and a unique key both guarantee uniqueness and both are backed by a unique index, so for lookups they behave alike, but they differ in identity, nullability, and count. A primary key is the chosen identity of the row. There is exactly one per table, it can never be null because an unknown identity is meaningless, and by convention foreign keys from other tables point at it, and in many databases it also determines the physical clustering of the data. It is the canonical handle by which the rest of the system refers to the row.

A unique key enforces that no two rows share the same value in a column or set of columns, but it is not the row's identity. A table can have many unique keys, and because the SQL standard treats null as unknown rather than equal to another null, a unique column generally permits a null value where a primary key cannot. So an accounts table can have the account id as its primary key and separate unique constraints on email and PAN, and a brand-new account with no email yet still inserts cleanly.

The senior point is the design choice. Even when a natural unique attribute like email exists, teams make the primary key a surrogate with no business meaning and keep email as a unique constraint, because the primary key must be stable and meaningless while business attributes change. Composite keys are also common, both as a composite primary key and as a composite unique constraint, for example unique on the pair of customer and account type to stop two savings accounts. At the National Bank of India the account id is the primary key that every transaction references, while email and PAN are unique constraints that forbid duplicates yet tolerate a not-yet-provided email. The line I always state is one primary key per table, never null, the identity and foreign-key target, versus many unique keys allowed, a null typically permitted, enforcing no-duplicates on other columns.
